composition.story: A diffusion model starts from pure random noise. At each of 50 steps, a U-Net looks at the noisy latent and the prompt, predicts the noise, and the scheduler subtracts part of it. Switch prompts: the same seed and noise schedule end in a different image, because the prompt steers every prediction.

aha.observation: Both prompts use the same seed and identical noise readouts, yet the decoded images differ. The prompt steers every noise prediction.

parts.presentation: Top rail. Steps already done are shown as trace on the rail. Previous and Next keep their names when disabled at the ends.
Pipeline left to right: prompt → text encoder → U-Net ⇄ scheduler loop on the latent → decoder → image.
Points to where the change happens. It shows no numbers.
Faint outline of the regions that were active in the previous step.
Cosine schedule: noise σ = cos(k/50·π/2), signal = sin(k/50·π/2), rounded to 2 decimals. Both prompts use the same scale.

controls.label: Step
controls.presentation: Previous / Next buttons, 9 states, moves one state at a time, keyboard arrows

controls.label: Prompt (same seed 42)
controls.presentation: Swaps the prompt variant. Seed, schedule and readouts stay fixed, so only the image changes.

controls.label: Reset
controls.presentation: Goes back to state s1 and the fox prompt

states.label: Encode prompt
states.sentence: The text encoder turns the prompt into an embedding the U-Net can read.
states.why: This embedding steers every later prediction.

states.label: Sample noise
states.sentence: Generation starts from pure random noise drawn from seed 42.
states.why: No image exists yet. Every pixel is noise.

states.label: Predict noise
states.sentence: The U-Net reads the noisy latent and the prompt, then estimates which part is noise.
states.why: It was trained to predict the noise that had been added to real images.

states.label: Subtract (step 1)
states.sentence: The scheduler subtracts only part of the predicted noise, giving a slightly cleaner latent.
states.why: Small steps keep the predictions reliable.

states.label: Step 10
states.sentence: After ten predict-and-subtract loops, a rough layout of colour appears.
states.why: Large shapes come out first, while the noise is still high.

states.label: Step 25
states.sentence: Halfway through, noise and signal are equal, and the subject's outline is clear.
states.why: Cosine schedule: σ and signal cross at k = 25.

states.label: Step 40
states.sentence: At low noise, the later steps refine fine detail.
states.why: Fine textures only show up once most of the noise is gone.

states.label: Step 50
states.sentence: After the last subtraction, the latent contains no noise.

states.label: Decode
states.sentence: The decoder turns the clean latent into pixels. Switch prompts to compare with the same seed.
states.why: Same seed and schedule. Only the prompt-guided predictions differ.

1.reason: The pipeline picture with a U-Net/scheduler loop and the prompt swap answers whether the prompt alone steers the final image from the same seed.

2.reason: The aha state s9 is the last state, reached only via the user-driven Next button, and it holds with identical readouts and a differing image.

3.reason: The step control moves through the states and the prompt select changes the image and latent descriptions while the noise readouts stay fixed, which is the intended comparison.

4.reason: The rail, picture, callout, ghost and readouts all bind to state/variant fields, and the callout regions and active lists exist in the declared regions.

6.reason: The story, state labels, callouts and controls consistently name the prompt, encoder, U-Net, scheduler, latent and decoder, along with seed 42 and the step counts.

7.reason: A single pipeline picture with one changing active set, one callout and four readouts per state adds the schedule mechanism without excess clutter.

8.reason: The cosine values check out at k=1, 10, 25, 40 and 50 (0.03, 0.31/0.95, 0.71/0.71 and 1.00), and the callouts locate while the readouts quantify, with only minor repetition of the latent text.
